source.title_on_document: Creative or Uncreative Partner: Comparing Humans and AI in Collaborative Creative Tasks

supplement.where: Referred to as 'supplementary information' (p. 4), 'SI 1' (p. 5), and 'SI 2' (p. 7); the document gives no URL. The preregistration is at https://osf.io/tveaf (p. 3). PDF pp. 20-27 hold only references.
supplement.holds: SI 1: the protocol for deriving a DAT score for ChatGPT-4o (p. 5). SI 2: further details of the story diversity analysis (p. 7). Also deviations from the preregistration and exploratory analyses not on the registry (p. 4). The main text prints coefficients with SEs for the AUT and story models and the test statistics of the diversity tests.

paper_design_summary: 208 Prolific participants were randomly assigned to work in alternating turns either with another participant (Human-Human, 68 pairs) or with a prompt-engineered GPT-4o partner (Human-AI, 72 pairs); turn order (Role A first, Role B second) was also randomly assigned. Each pair did two Alternate Uses Task trials (bottle, book; 3 minutes each) and a 10-minute short story written one sentence per turn, and then each person did the Divergent Association Task alone. Outputs were scored automatically: AUT originality with CLAUS, story originality with divergent semantic integration, elaboration as word count, and diversity as the variance of originality scores, forward flow between consecutive ideas, and a Sentence-BERT diversity contribution score across stories.

studies.label: Collaborative AUT and short story with a human or a GPT-4o partner (Prolific)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Partner type: a prompt-engineered GPT-4o partner (Human-AI) or another participant (Human-Human). Turn role (Role A initiates, Role B goes second) was also randomly assigned and kept across tasks; in Human-AI pairs the AI took the other role.
assignment.quote: Upon taking part in the study, participants were randomly assigned to either a human-AI (72 pairs) or human-human (68 pairs) condition.
assignment.locator: p. 4, Methods, Participants (partner condition); p. 4, Materials and Procedure (role); p. 1, Abstract
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 3, Methods: 'pre-registered on the Open Science Framework (OSF)', https://osf.io/tveaf

arms.name: Human-AI
arms.description: The participant takes turns with a prompt-engineered GPT-4o partner in a chat interface built to look like the human-partner interface; the AI replies after a fixed delay (5 s on the AUT, 10 s on the story). Participants were told before the tasks that their partner was an AI.

arms.name: Human-Human
arms.description: The participant takes turns with another Prolific participant, matched through SMARTRIQS, in the matching chat interface. Participants were told before the tasks that their partner was human.

participants.exclusions: The paper removed the data of participants who admitted using external internet or AI resources (honesty check, p. 6) but does not say how many. Three printed counts agree: 208 recruited and randomly assigned (72 Human-AI pairs, 68 Human-Human pairs; p. 4), 208 analyzed in Table 1 (AI 72, Human 136; p. 7), and 72 and 68 pairs in the story diversity test (p. 15). So either no one was removed or these are counts after removal. The paper does not say which. n_analyzed (208; 72 and 136) holds for Table 1 and the story diversity test. The AUT mixed models analyze fewer people, and the paper prints no people count for them. They have 2,970 responses in 139 groups (Base and Covariates) and 2,066 human responses in 137 groups (Human-Only; Tables 2 and 3). The Levene tests use 3,038 and 2,134 responses (F(1, 3036) and F(1, 2132), p. 11). Both pairs of counts differ by 904, the GPT-4o responses, so the Human-Only models keep every human response of the other models, and 2 of the 139 groups hold only GPT-4o responses. The human responses in all AUT models therefore come from 137 of the 140 pairs: between 137 and 205 people, at most 70 of them in the Human-AI arm. The models also drop 68 responses that the Levene tests keep. The paper explains neither gap.
participants.who: Prolific participants; mean age 35.18 (SD 12.07); 54.8 percent female; 97.1 percent with English as first language; paid $6 for about 30 minutes.
participants.quote: A total of 208 participants were recruited from Prolific for the study.

ai_tool.name_model: GPT-4o (called 'ChatGPT-4o' in the paper), accessed via the OpenAI API through PythonAnywhere
ai_tool.how_used: Turn-taking co-creator: the prompted model alternated with the participant and contributed its own AUT ideas and story sentences, as Role A or Role B, in a chat interface built to look like the human-partner interface, with fixed response delays (5 s on the AUT, 10 s on the story). The prompts carried explicit constraints and instructions to make it a creative collaborator. Pair-level scores include the AI's contributions unless the human-only models remove them. Coded 'other' because the AI co-creates as a partner; the closest codes are ideas_supplied and open_chat.

task.description: Two collaborative tasks in one session, taking turns: (1) the Alternate Uses Task for 'bottle' and 'book', alternating ideas, with 'pass' typed after 30 seconds without an idea (divergent_test); (2) a short story from the words 'stamp-letter-send', one sentence per turn (creative_writing). Afterward each participant did the Divergent Association Task alone, then questionnaires on partner perception, AI attitudes, personality, and demographics.
task.duration: AUT 3 minutes per object (two objects); story 10 minutes; whole study about 30 minutes

outcomes.name: AUT originality, all responses in the pair (including the AI's responses)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Originality of each AUT response scored by CLAUS (Cross-Lingual Alternate Uses Scoring), a transformer model fine-tuned to match human ratings, on the Creativity Assessment Platform (p. 5). Book and bottle pooled. In the Human-AI arm the scored set includes GPT-4o's own responses: 904 of the 2,970 (2,970 minus the 2,066 human-only responses, Table 2; also 3,038 minus 2,134 from the Levene degrees of freedom, p. 11), about 54 percent of that arm's roughly 1,678 responses (72 pairs x 23.3 responses, p. 9). The paper says these responses 'may have previously masked underlying differences in human responses' (p. 10). The record keeps question with_ai because both arms score the pair's pooled output, but S1-O2 scores only the participants' own responses and is the form's recommended with_ai record (open question 1). Converging model: originality ~ condition * role + dat_scaled + (1|groupID) + (1|groupID:ResponseId); the preregistered random-slope model and a reduced random-slope model failed to converge (p. 9). Robustness variant: the Covariates model adds item, fluency (ideas per pair), and word count (Table 2), recorded as the second contrast. Reference categories: Condition = AI-Human, Role = A, so a negative Condition (Human-Human) coefficient means higher originality with the AI partner.

contrasts.reported: Base model (Model 1): Condition (Human-Human) B = -0.065*** (SE 0.007), t = -9.69, p < .001; Role B 0.018*** (0.004), t = 4.22; Condition x Role B -0.021** (0.007), t = -2.87, p = .005; DAT (scaled) 0.021*** (0.002). Reference: Condition = AI-Human, Role = A. N observations 2,970; N groups 139. Predicted values with 95% CIs only in Figure 2a.
contrasts.locator: pp. 9-10, Table 2 (Base column); p. 10, text; p. 11, Figure 2a

Predicted values with 95% CIs only in Figure 2b.

outcomes.name: Variance of AUT originality scores, all responses (Levene's test)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Levene's test with the median as center, comparing the variance of CLAUS originality scores between conditions (p. 11). The degrees of freedom imply 3,038 responses, 904 of them GPT-4o's (about 54 percent of the Human-AI arm's responses), and the paper says the difference was 'predominantly driven by the AI’s responses' (p. 11). The paper names this test and forward flow as the two tests of hypothesis 2 (p. 6; p. 11), so primary is paper_primary, as for S1-O5; whether the preregistration lists it is not stated. The paper labels it a diversity analysis ('the range of originality score'), but it measures the spread of a quality score, not similarity of content across people. The human-only version is S1-O4.

contrasts.reported: Levene F(1, 3036) = 3.72, p = .054, called 'a marginal significant difference' (p. 11); Figure 3a title: F = 3.72, p = 0.0538. The Discussion reads it as 'a wider range of originality scores for human-AI pairs', driven by the AI's responses (p. 17). No arm variances printed; distributions only in Figure 3a.
contrasts.locator: p. 11, Diversity; p. 12, Figure 3a; p. 17, Discussion

outcomes.measure_detail: Levene's test as in S1-O3 with the AI's responses removed.

contrasts.reported: Levene F(1, 2132) = 0.15, p = .70; Figure 3b title: F = 0.15, p = 0.696. Distributions only in Figure 3b.

outcomes.name: AUT forward flow (semantic distance between consecutive ideas in the pair's sequence), all responses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Semantic distance = 1 minus cosine similarity between consecutive responses within each pair's sequence, from paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2 sentence embeddings (pp. 6-7). Linear regression of semantic distance on condition, idea sequence position, and their interaction; first 20 ideas per pair; 'pass' kept as a response (p. 12). Consecutive ideas alternate between the two partners, so this is variety within a pair's own sequence, not similarity across pairs; coded flexibility. In Human-AI pairs each distance therefore joins one of the participant's turns and one of GPT-4o's, and GPT-4o's responses are about 54 percent of the Human-AI arm's scored AUT responses (see S1-O1). The paper calls it a diversity measure (hypothesis 2). The text cites 'figure 3a' for this result; the plot is Figure 4a.

contrasts.reported: Main effect of condition B = 0.091, SE = 0.094, t = 6.34, p < .001 (as printed; Human-Human pairs show higher semantic distance); running idea sequence B = 0.003, SE = 0.001, t = 2.43, p = .015; interaction described as 'a no significant interaction (p = .015)'. Arm-level semantic distance only in Figure 4a.
contrasts.locator: p. 12, forward flow paragraph; p. 12, Figure 4a

outcomes.question: with_ai

contrasts.reported: Main effect of condition B = 0.064, SE = 0.024, t = 2.65, 'p < .008'; running sequence p = .47; interaction p = .34. Human participants in Human-Human pairs show stable higher semantic distance (Figure 4b).

outcomes.name: AUT elaboration (word count per response), all responses
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Word count per AUT response, a computed count (coded automated_score as in earlier reconciled forms). Converging model: word count ~ condition * participant role + dat_scaled + (1|groupID) + (1|groupID:ResponseId), after the preregistered model failed to converge (p. 12). Robustness variant: the Covariates model adds item and fluency (Table 3; the table note also lists word count, which is the outcome). The human-only version is S1-O8. In the Human-AI arm the scored set includes GPT-4o's 904 responses, about 54 percent of that arm's responses (see S1-O1). Reference categories: Condition = AI-Human, Role = A. Pair-level descriptives: 3.34 words per idea in Human-Human pairs, 12.7 in Human-AI pairs (p. 9).

outcomes.name: Short story originality (divergent semantic integration, DSI)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: DSI: semantic distance between all pairs of words in the story text (Johnson et al., 2022) (p. 5). Linear mixed model with condition, participant role, scaled DAT, and a random effect of group ID; robustness variant adds word count (pp. 14-15). Each pair wrote one story, so the role and DAT predictors and the group random effect imply one row per participant within a pair, and the paper reads the role terms as differences between participants ('Role B participants produced less original content only when partnered with a human', p. 17). The Methods describe DSI as a score of the story text (p. 5). Whether each row's DSI covers the whole co-written story (with GPT-4o's sentences in Human-AI pairs) or only that participant's sentences, whether GPT-4o has rows of its own, and the number of observations are not stated. The text gives no reference category; the predicted values in Figure 6a are consistent with a Human-AI reference (intercept 0.812 at Human-AI, Role A), as in Tables 2 and 3.

contrasts.reported: Initial model: intercept B = 0.812 (SE 0.005), t = 151.86; condition B = -0.006, SE = 0.008, t = -0.79, p = .431; role B = 0.003, SE = 0.007, t = 0.43, p = .667; DAT B = 0.001, SE = 0.003, p = .795; condition x role B = -0.019, SE = 0.010, t = -1.83, p = .070. With word count: condition B = 0.006, SE = 0.008, t = 0.72, p = .472; role B = 0.006, SE = 0.007, p = .393; condition x role B = -0.020, SE = 0.010, t = -2.03, p = .045; word count B = 0.0002, SE = 0.00006, t = 4.05. Predicted values only in Figure 6.
contrasts.locator: pp. 14-15, Creative Short Story Task, Originality; p. 15, Figure 6

outcomes.name: Short story diversity (diversity contribution score across stories)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Sentence-BERT (paraphrase-multilingual-MiniLM-L12-v2) embeddings; a condition's diversity = mean pairwise cosine dissimilarity (1 - cosine similarity) among all stories in the condition; each story's diversity contribution = total diversity minus the diversity computed without that story (p. 7). Compared with the Mann-Whitney U test because both distributions failed normality, and with a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. n_units = 140 stories: the test's group sizes are 72 and 68 pairs, one story per pair (p. 15); the paper does not print the total. Stories are co-written (one person and GPT-4o in Human-AI, two people in Human-Human). As the main text describes it, the contribution is computed within each condition, so it averages exactly zero over a condition's stories whatever that condition's diversity: the mean of the leave-one-out means equals the full mean. The U and D tests therefore compare the shapes of two zero-mean distributions (Figure 7a centers both near 0) and cannot show which condition's stories are more alike. The paper prints no condition-level diversity score.

contrasts.reported: Mann-Whitney U = 2674, p = 0.347 (Human-AI n = 72 pairs, Human-Human n = 68 pairs); Kolmogorov-Smirnov D = 0.217, p = 0.061. Shapiro-Wilk: Human-Human W = 0.856, p < 0.001; Human-AI W = 0.946, p = 0.004. No arm medians, means, or condition-level diversity printed; distributions only in Figure 7a. Direction is coded no_clear_difference only because no level comparison is printed: the contribution scores average zero within each condition by construction, so these tests cannot show which condition's stories are more alike.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Data Analysis; p. 15, Diversity; p. 15, Figure 7a

diversity_detail.metric: Leave-one-out diversity contribution: the condition's mean pairwise cosine dissimilarity (1 - cosine similarity) minus the same quantity computed without the focal story
diversity_detail.computed_over: All pairs of stories within a condition; each story's contribution to its condition's diversity
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Mann-Whitney U test and two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on story-level contribution scores; no standard error or interval. The scores average zero within each condition by construction, so the tests compare distribution shapes, not levels of diversity.
diversity_detail.notes: One story per pair; Human-AI stories are written by one person and GPT-4o, Human-Human stories by two people. Further details in SI 2 (not in this PDF) and Luchini et al. (2025). The printed U = 2674 with groups of 72 and 68 gives a normal-approximation p of about 0.35, consistent with the printed p = 0.347. No condition-level diversity (mean pairwise dissimilarity within each condition) is printed, so this record supplies no across_people difference; SI 2 may give it (open question 13).

outcomes.name: Short story forward flow (semantic distance between consecutive sentences), exploratory
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Exploratory forward flow over the sentence sequence: semantic distance between consecutive sentences regressed on condition, running sentence sequence, and their interaction (p. 15). F(3, 1762) implies 1,766 distances. The text and Figure 7b describe 'human participants'; whether AI-written sentences are excluded is not stated.

contrasts.reported: Condition B = 0.002, SE = 0.016, t = 0.17, p = .90; running sequence B = 0.001, SE = 0.001, t = 1.50, p = .14; condition x sequence B = 0.004, SE = 0.002, t = 2.37, p = .018; R2 = .014, F(3, 1762) = 8.60, p < .001. The text describes the Human-AI distance as stable and the Human-Human distance as rising across sentences, which fits only a Human-AI reference: the modeled Human-Human minus Human-AI gap is 0.002 at the start (not significant) and grows by 0.004 per sentence. The fitted lines in Figure 7b cross near the first sentences, inside overlapping bands. The Discussion reads the result as higher semantic jumps with a human partner (p. 18).
contrasts.locator: p. 15, paragraph after Diversity; p. 15, Figure 7b; p. 18, Discussion, Hypothesis 2

outcomes.name: Short story elaboration (story word count)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Story word count (p. 16); linear mixed model with condition, participant role, scaled DAT, and a random effect of group ID. As for S1-O10, the rows are participants within pairs: the paper reads the role term as a difference between participants ('role B participants used fewer words than role A participants', p. 16), and the Discussion reads the story result as longer human responses with an AI partner, most for Role A (p. 18). Whether each row counts the whole co-written story or only that participant's sentences, and whether GPT-4o has rows, is not stated. A computed count, coded automated_score as in S1-O7. The predicted values in Figure 8 are consistent with a Human-AI reference (intercept 133.36 at Human-AI, Role A).

contrasts.reported: Intercept B = 133.36, SE = 5.34, t = 24.97; condition B = -48.38, SE = 7.68, t = -6.30, p < .001 ('human-human interactions producing significantly fewer words compared to the AI condition'); role B = -12.04, SE = 5.59, t = -2.15, p = .033; DAT B = 8.44, SE = 2.61, t = 3.24, p = .001; condition x role B = 7.14, SE = 8.05, t = 0.89, p = .377. Predicted values only in Figure 8.

outcomes.name: Divergent Association Task score, taken alone after the collaborative tasks
outcomes.question: after_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Divergent Association Task: 10 unrelated words; score = mean pairwise semantic distance (GloVe, Common Crawl) x 100 (p. 5). Completed individually, without the partner, after the collaborative tasks (p. 4). The paper uses it as a covariate of baseline verbal creative ability, not as an outcome, and prints only arm means. Construct coded flexibility under the codebook rule 'Variety among one person's own ideas is flexibility': the score measures how far apart one participant's own words are. This follows the final c097 and the reconciled c126; c069 codes the DAT as other, and the codebook's flexibility row counts categories, so Review 1 should set one code for the DAT (open question 11).
outcomes.delay: Same session, after the collaborative tasks

contrasts.reported: Humans in the paired (Human-Human) group: average DAT 75.4; humans in the AI group: 76.7. No SD, n, or test printed; the paper does not compare the arms on DAT.

eligibility.reason: Participants were randomly assigned to a GPT-4o partner or to a human partner, with no AI in the human condition (p. 4), so criterion 1 is met with an ai_vs_active comparison (a human partner is another aid). 208 people were randomized (72 Human-AI, 136 Human-Human; p. 4). All 208 are analyzed in Table 1 (p. 7) and in the story diversity test, which uses all 72 and 68 pairs (p. 15). The AUT mixed models draw human responses from 137 of the 140 pairs, so they analyze between 137 and 205 people (Tables 2 and 3). Criterion 2 is met by a wide margin. Every outcome is a computed score of produced text (CLAUS originality, DSI, word count, forward flow, Sentence-BERT diversity, DAT), so criterion 3 is met. It holds through S1-O2 alone, which scores only the participants' own AUT responses (Table 2, Human-Only). Caveats: GPT-4o's own responses are about 54 percent of the Human-AI arm's responses in the all-responses AUT records, each Human-Human output has two human contributors, the story diversity test cannot show which arm's stories are more alike, and no outcome is rated by people.

one_line_finding: With a GPT-4o partner instead of a human partner, AUT originality scored over all pair responses, GPT-4o's included (2,970 responses, 2,066 without GPT-4o's), was higher (Human-Human minus Human-AI B = -0.065, SE 0.007), did not differ once word count, fluency, and item were controlled (B = 0.010, SE 0.008, p = .201), and was lower for the participants' own responses (B = 0.029, SE 0.010, p = .005; Table 2, pp. 9-10).
open_questions: Which AUT originality record is the with_ai primary record? S1-O1 is the preregistered model, but about 54 percent of the Human-AI arm's scored responses are GPT-4o's own (904 of about 1,678, computed from Table 2, the Levene degrees of freedom, and p. 9). S1-O2 scores only the participants' own responses, and the form recommends it. Codebook section 8 rule 1 would otherwise pick S1-O1. The same choice applies to elaboration (S1-O7 vs S1-O8).

Human-only originality and elaboration are printed only from models with item, fluency, and (for originality) word-count covariates (Tables 2 and 3), and word count and fluency differ by condition (p. 9). A human-only estimate without these covariates is not printed. Which specification the extraction uses is open.

AUT forward flow (all responses): the condition effect is printed as B = 0.091, SE = 0.094, t = 6.34 (p. 12); the SE and t cannot both be right. The interaction is called non-significant with p = .015, and the text cites 'figure 3a' for a plot that appears as Figure 4a.

AUT forward flow (S1-O5) and Levene's test (S1-O3) are coded paper_primary because the paper names them as the two tests of hypothesis 2 (p. 6; p. 11). The main text does not say whether the preregistration lists them, and the SI that would note deviations is not on file.

Forward flow measures distance between consecutive ideas within a pair, so it is coded flexibility rather than across_people diversity. In the human-only AUT forward flow, consecutive human ideas come from one person in Human-AI pairs but alternate between two people in Human-Human pairs. This is a reading of the design; the paper does not discuss it.

Levene (all responses) is coded no_clear_difference at p = .054, following the c007 reconciliation for p-values just above .05. The paper reads it as a wider range of originality scores for Human-AI pairs.

Table 2 and Table 3 notes say the base model includes 'date' (likely DAT) and give the item reference as 'Brick', though the items were book and bottle. The Table 3 note lists word count as a covariate of the word-count model, and the Table 2 significance key is garbled ('p < .05. *p < .01. **p < .001').

The number of participants removed under the honesty check is not stated. The AUT mixed models draw human responses from 137 of the 140 pairs (between 137 and 205 people, at most 70 in the Human-AI arm), 2 of their 139 groups hold only GPT-4o responses, and they drop 68 responses that the Levene tests keep (2,970 vs 3,038; 2,066 vs 2,134). The paper explains neither gap.

The story DSI and word-count models (S1-O10, S1-O13) have one row per participant within pairs, but the paper does not say whether each row's score covers the whole story or only that participant's sentences, or whether GPT-4o has rows. The text gives no reference category for the story models; Figures 6a and 8 are consistent with Human-AI as the reference.

The DAT was taken alone after the collaborative tasks (p. 4) yet is used as a baseline covariate in every model. It is recorded as an after_ai outcome, but only arm means (76.7 vs 75.4) are printed, with no SD, n, or test.
The DAT is coded flexibility, as in the final c097 and the reconciled c126; c069 codes it as other, and the codebook's flexibility row counts categories. Review 1 should set one code for the DAT.

The control arm is a human partner, not a solo worker, and each Human-Human output has two human contributors. Whether this ai_vs_active contrast fits the pooled with_ai comparisons is a Review 1 question.

Story diversity (S1-O11): as the main text describes it, the leave-one-out contribution scores average zero within each condition by construction, so the Mann-Whitney and Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests compare distribution shapes and cannot show which condition's stories are more alike. No condition-level diversity is printed. SI 2 (not on file) may give it or describe the computation differently.

Word-count measure code: no codebook measure fits a plain word count (S1-O7, S1-O8, S1-O13). The record uses automated_score, as other forms do (final c026 and c052). This is a Review 1 codebook decision.

The paper does not describe the allocation mechanism or what happened when SMARTRIQS could not match a participant with a partner. The split of 72 to 136 people fits equal numbers of pairs per arm, and criterion 1 rests on the stated random assignment (p. 4).
notes: One experiment: the same participants did both collaborative tasks. task.type is divergent_test for the AUT; the story outcomes S1-O10 to S1-O13 are creative_writing. Human-only models are separate outcomes because they score a different set of outputs (the person's own responses); covariate-adjusted models are robustness variants inside an outcome. Role A/B was also randomized and interacts with condition in several models; the interactions are in the reported strings, not separate contrasts. The all-responses AUT records (S1-O1, S1-O3, S1-O5, S1-O7, S1-O9) score the pair's pooled responses, and in the Human-AI arm about 54 percent of them are GPT-4o's own (904 of about 1,678, computed from Table 2, the Levene degrees of freedom, and the per-pair counts on p. 9). They keep question with_ai under the form-spec rule, but S1-O2 is the record that scores only what participants produced, and the form recommends it as the with_ai primary record for Review 1 to confirm. The story DSI and word-count models (S1-O10, S1-O13) have one row per participant within pairs. The story diversity contribution scores (S1-O11) average zero within each condition by construction, so their test does not compare the arms' levels of diversity. Self-reported partner perceptions (creativity, cooperativeness, ease of collaboration, connection, Inclusion of Other in Self) and AI attitudes are not scored on output and are omitted. Page numbers are PDF pages; the document prints none. The story diversity method follows Luchini et al. (2025), screened as c159, which recruited Penn State students; no shared participants are stated.

challenge_resolution.what_changed: Confirmed: the main text computes diversity 'for each condition' over 'all responses in a condition' (p. 7), and the mean of the leave-one-out means equals the full mean, so the contributions average exactly zero in each condition. A numerical check with two simulated pools of diversity 0.095 and 0.998 gave a mean contribution of 0 in both, and Figure 7a centers both arms near 0. measure_detail, reported, and diversity_detail (uncertainty, notes) now say that the tests cannot show which condition's stories are more alike and that the paper prints no condition-level diversity. direction stays no_clear_difference, the only code that claims no direction, and reported says what it means here. open_items.item: With_ai primary record (open question 1): S1-O1, the preregistered model, scores pooled pair responses, about 54 percent of them GPT-4o's in the Human-AI arm. S1-O2 scores only the participants' own responses, and the form recommends it. Criterion 3 holds through either. Review 1 decides.

Covariates (open question 2): human-only originality and elaboration are printed only from models that control for fluency and, for originality, word count, both of which differ by condition. An estimate without them is not printed.
AUT forward-flow typos (open question 3): SE = 0.094 with t = 6.34, an interaction called non-significant at p = .015, and 'figure 3a' for Figure 4a (p. 12).
Preregistered status of forward flow and Levene's test (open question 4): coded paper_primary because the paper names them as the tests of hypothesis 2. The SI notes deviations from the registry.
Forward flow as flexibility, and two contributors in the human-only Human-Human sequence (open question 5): a coding reading of the design.
Levene's test at p = .054 coded no_clear_difference (open question 6): a coding convention from c007.

Table 2 and 3 notes ('date', 'Brick', word count as a covariate of word count, garbled significance key; open question 7). The coded contrasts use the printed B and SE, so nothing depends on the notes.

People in the AUT mixed models and honesty-check removals (open question 8): between 137 and 205 people, 2 groups with only GPT-4o responses, and 68 responses dropped relative to the Levene tests, with no counts printed. Criterion 2 holds under any reading (208 in Table 1 and the story diversity test).

Story model rows (open question 9): one row per participant, but whether each row's DSI or word count covers the whole story or only that participant's sentences, and whether GPT-4o has rows, is not stated.
DAT arm comparison (open question 10): only means (76.7 vs 75.4), with no SD, n, or test; the DAT was taken after the collaborative tasks and serves as a covariate in every model.
DAT construct code (open question 11): coded flexibility as in c097 and c126; c069 uses other. Review 1 sets one code.

Human-partner control arm (open question 12): whether the ai_vs_active contrast, with two human contributors per control output, fits pooled with_ai comparisons. Criterion 1 accepts a comparison group that works without AI.

Story diversity level (open question 13): the contribution scores average zero within each condition by construction, and no condition-level diversity is printed, so no across_people difference is available. Criterion 3 holds through other outcomes.
Word-count measure code (open question 14 and the rejected outcome-lens problem): no codebook measure fits, and the record keeps automated_score as other forms do. A Review 1 codebook decision.

Allocation mechanism (open question 15): not described, nor what happened when no partner could be matched. The 72 to 136 split of people fits equal pairs per arm, and criterion 1 rests on the stated random assignment.
